questions.prompt: Which statement correctly explains how the unit circle defines cos t and sin t for every real number t?
questions.prompt_markup: Which statement correctly explains how the unit circle defines cos t and sin t for every real number t?

choices.text: Start at (1, 0) and move t units straight up; cos t and sin t are the coordinates of the point reached.
Start at (1, 0) and travel |t| units along the unit circle, counterclockwise if t > 0 and clockwise if t < 0; cos t and sin t are the x- and y-coordinates of the endpoint.
Travel t units counterclockwise from (1, 0); for t < 0 the values are undefined.
Draw a right triangle with an acute angle of t radians; cos t and sin t are the ratios adjacent/hypotenuse and opposite/hypotenuse, so the definition works only for t between 0 and π/2.

questions.correct_answer: Start at (1, 0) and travel |t| units along the unit circle, counterclockwise if t > 0 and clockwise if t < 0; cos t and sin t are the x- and y-coordinates of the endpoint.
questions.grading_note: Arc length |t| from (1, 0), direction by the sign of t, coordinates of the endpoint. The others use the right-triangle definition (only acute angles), move along a line instead of the circle (the point leaves the circle), or leave negative t undefined.

questions.prompt: Which explanation shows why sin(t + 2π) = sin t for every real number t?
questions.prompt_markup: Which explanation shows why sin(t + 2π) = sin t for every real number t?

choices.text: For t = π/2 both sides equal 1, so they are always equal.
Sine distributes over addition, so sin(t + 2π) = sin t + sin 2π, and sin 2π = 0 because the point at 2π is (1, 0); therefore sin(t + 2π) = sin t.
Adding 2π to t reflects the endpoint on the unit circle over the x-axis, and a reflection over the x-axis keeps the y-coordinate, so sin(t + 2π) = sin t.
The unit circle has circumference 2π, so adding 2π adds one full trip around it: t and t + 2π end at the same point, which has the same y-coordinate.

questions.correct_answer: The unit circle has circumference 2π, so adding 2π adds one full trip around it: t and t + 2π end at the same point, which has the same y-coordinate.
questions.grading_note: One full turn returns to the same point. The others distribute sine over a sum (false in general), check one value, or describe the wrong motion.

cos(2π/3) = -1/2, so cos t is negative on this interval.
On the unit circle cos t decreases steadily as t increases from 0, so once t passes π/2, where cos t = 0, the value of cos t is negative for every larger t.

questions.prompt: Why is -1 ≤ sin t ≤ 1 for every real number t?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is -1 ≤ sin t ≤ 1 for every real number t?

choices.text: sin(π/2) = 1 and sin(3π/2) = -1, so every value lies between them.
In a right triangle the hypotenuse is longer than either leg, so opposite/hypotenuse is less than 1, which means sin t < 1 for every real number t.
sin t is the y-coordinate of a point on the unit circle x² + y² = 1, so y² ≤ 1, which means -1 ≤ y ≤ 1.
sin t is an arc length on the unit circle, and those arcs are at most 1.

questions.correct_answer: sin t is the y-coordinate of a point on the unit circle x² + y² = 1, so y² ≤ 1, which means -1 ≤ y ≤ 1.
questions.grading_note: Coordinates of points on the unit circle satisfy x² + y² = 1. The others only cover acute angles (and wrongly exclude sin t = 1), misstate the definition, or reason from two values.

questions.prompt: Why is cos an even function?
questions.prompt_markup: Why is cos an even function?

choices.text: The points for t and -t are reflections over the x-axis, which keeps the x-coordinate, so cos(-t) = cos t.
The points for t and -t are reflections over the y-axis, which keeps the x-coordinate, so cos(-t) = cos t.
cos t is positive for every t, so cos(-t) and cos t are always equal.
The points for t and -t are reflections over the x-axis, which negates the x-coordinate, so cos(-t) = -cos t.

questions.correct_answer: The points for t and -t are reflections over the x-axis, which keeps the x-coordinate, so cos(-t) = cos t.
questions.grading_note: Reflecting over the x-axis changes only the sign of the y-coordinate. The others name the wrong reflection, use a false fact (cos is not always positive), or say the x-coordinate changes sign.
